'''''Peter Pan''''' is a 1953 American animated [[fantasy adventure film]] produced by [[Walt Disney Productions]] and released by [[RKO Radio Pictures]]. Based on [[J. M. Barrie]]'s 1904 play [[Peter Pan (play and novel)|of the same name]], the film was directed by [[Hamilton Luske]], [[Clyde Geronimi]], and [[Wilfred Jackson]]. Featuring the voices of [[Bobby Driscoll]], [[Kathryn Beaumont]], [[Hans Conried]], [[Bill Thompson (voice actor)|Bill Thompson]], [[Heather Angel (actress)|Heather Angel]], [[Paul Collins (actor)|Paul Collins]], Tommy Luske, [[Candy Candido]], [[Tom Conway]], [[Roland Dupree]] and [[Don Barclay (actor)|Don Barclay]], the film's plot follows [[Wendy Darling]] and her two brothers, who meet the eternally-young [[Peter Pan (character)|Peter Pan]] and travel with him to the island of [[Neverland|Never Land]] to stay young, where they also have to face Peter's archenemy, [[Captain Hook]].

In 1935, [[Walt Disney]] began considering plans to adapt Barrie's play into an animated feature. He purchased the film rights from [[Paramount Pictures]] in 1938, and began preliminary development in the next year. However, following the [[attack on Pearl Harbor]], Disney shelved the project when his studio was contracted by the United States government to produce training and war propaganda films. The project sat idle in development for the rest of the decade until it experienced a [[Turnaround (filmmaking)|turnaround]] in 1949. To assist the animators, live-action reference footage was shot with actors on soundstages. It also marked the last Disney film in which all nine members of [[Disney's Nine Old Men]] worked together as directing animators.

''Peter Pan'' was released on February 5, 1953, becoming the final Disney animated feature released through RKO before Disney founded [[Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures|his own distribution company]]. The film was entered into the [[1953 Cannes Film Festival]],<ref name="festival-cannes.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/3894/year/1953.html |title=Festival de Cannes: Peter Pan |access-date=January 23, 2009 |work=Cannes Film Festival |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110822155433/http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/3894/year/1953.html |archive-date=August 22, 2011}}</ref> Upon its release, the film earned generally positive reviews from film critics and was a box office success. Its representation of the Native Americans received retrospective criticism.

A sequel, titled ''[[Return to Never Land]]'', was released in 2002, and a [[Tinker Bell (film series)|series of direct-to-DVD prequels]] focusing on [[Tinker Bell (Disney character)|Tinker Bell]] began in 2008. A television series featuring the characters, ''[[Jake and the Never Land Pirates]]'', was released in 2015. A [[Peter Pan & Wendy (film)|live-action adaptation]] of the film was released on [[Disney+]] in 2023.

==Plot==
<!--Per WP:FILMPLOT, plot should be between 400 and 700 words. Please check word count before adding anything. Current count 567-->
In [[Edwardian]] London 1904, George and Mary Darling's preparations to attend a party are disrupted by the antics of their boys, John and Michael, who are acting out a [[Peter Pan (character)|Peter Pan]] story told to them by their elder sister [[Wendy Darling|Wendy]]. An irritated George demands that Wendy drop the stories and move out of the nursery, since "sooner or later, people have to grow up" and also chains Nana the female dog outside because she is a dog and not a nurse. Later that night, Peter himself arrives in the nursery to find his lost shadow. He persuades Wendy to come to [[Neverland|Never Land]], where she will never have to grow up, and she and the boys fly there with the begrudging help of the pixie [[Tinker Bell (Disney character)|Tinker Bell]].

A ship of [[pirate]]s is anchored off Never Land, led by [[Captain Hook]] and his first mate, [[Mr. Smee (Disney)|Mr. Smee]]. Hook wants revenge on Peter for cutting off his hand, but fears the crocodile which consumed the hand, knowing it is eager to eat the rest of him. When Pan and the Darlings arrive, Hook shoots at them with a cannon, and Peter sends the Darlings off to safety while he baits the pirates. Tinker Bell, who is jealous of Peter's attention to Wendy, convinces the [[Lost Boys (Peter Pan)|Lost Boys]] that Peter has ordered them to shoot down Wendy. Tinker Bell's treachery is soon found out, and Peter [[banishment|banishes]] her for a week. John and Michael set off with the Lost Boys to find the island's [[Indigenous peoples|Indians]]; however, the Indians capture the group, believing them to be responsible for taking the chief's daughter, [[Tiger Lily (Peter Pan)|Tiger Lily]].

Meanwhile, Peter takes Wendy to see the [[mermaid]]s, who flee in terror when Hook arrives on the scene. Peter and Wendy see that Hook and Smee have captured Tiger Lily, to force her to disclose the location of Peter's hideout. Peter frees Tiger Lily and returns her to the Chief, and the tribe honors Peter. Meanwhile, Hook takes advantage of Tinker Bell's jealousy of Wendy, tricking the fairy into revealing Peter's secret hideout instead.

Wendy and her brothers eventually grow homesick and plan to return to London. They invite Peter and the Lost Boys to join them and be adopted by the Darlings. The Lost Boys agree, but Peter does not want to grow up and refuses. The pirates lie in wait, and capture the Lost Boys and the Darlings as they exit the lair, leaving behind a [[time bomb]] to kill Peter. Hook attempts to persuade his captives to join the crew, threatening to make them [[walk the plank]] if they refuse. Tinker Bell learns of the plot, just in time to snatch the bomb from Peter as it explodes.

Peter rescues Tinker Bell from the rubble, and together they rescue Wendy, confronting the pirates and releasing the children. Peter engages Hook in combat as the children fight off the crew, and defeats him. Hook falls into the sea and swims away, pursued by the crocodile. Peter commandeers the deserted ship and, assisted by Tinker Bell's pixie dust, flies it to London with the children aboard although the Lost Boys choose to stay with Peter Pan in Neverland.

George and Mary Darling return home and find Wendy sleeping at the nursery's open window. Wendy awakens and excitedly tells about their adventures and that she's ready to grow up but her father who has softened up tells her she can stay in the nursery and even brings Nana back inside. The parents look out the window and see Hook's pirate ship in the clouds. George recognizes the ship, implying that he himself went to Neverland when he was a boy.

[[Walt Disney]] was familiar with [[J. M. Barrie]]'s play ''[[Peter Pan (play and novel)|Peter Pan, or the Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up]]'' since childhood,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://d23.com/peter-pan-takes-flight-in-a-disney-movie-club-exclusive-anniversary-edition/|title=''Peter Pan'' Takes Flight in a Disney Movie Club Exclusive Anniversary Edition|website=[[D23 (Disney)|D23]]|date=June 15, 2023 |access-date=November 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230617031139/https://d23.com/peter-pan-takes-flight-in-a-disney-movie-club-exclusive-anniversary-edition/|archive-date=June 17, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> having seen a touring production starring [[Maude Adams]] at the Cater Opera House in [[Marceline, Missouri]],{{sfn|Burnes|Viets|Butler|2002|page=24}} in 1913.<ref name="YouCanFly">{{cite AV media|title=You Can Fly!: The Making of Peter Pan|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XM2Md6Ctil0|type=Documentary film|publisher=Walt Disney Home Video|year=1998|via=YouTube|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230525043035/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XM2Md6Ctil0|archive-date=May 25, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1935, he first expressed interest in adapting the play{{sfn|Koenig|1997|page=94}} as his second animated feature film after ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]'',<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas">{{cite video|title=The Peter Pan That Almost Was|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F4DVVpJt6l8|type=Bonus feature|location=''Peter Pan'' Platinum Edition DVD|publisher=[[Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment]]|year=2007|via=[[YouTube]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230326030715/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F4DVVpJt6l8|archive-date=March 26, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> which was still in production at the time.<ref name="YouCanFly" /> During his acquisition spree in [[Europe]] in April 1938, [[Roy O. Disney]] went to [[London]] to acquire the rights from the [[Great Ormond Street Hospital|Great Ormond Street Hospital for Sick Children]], but [[Paramount Pictures]] had already secured the live-action screen rights. The hospital unsuccessfully offered to have Disney and Paramount make an agreement;{{sfn|Gabler|2006|page=283}} however, by October of that year, Walt had purchased the animation rights from Paramount{{sfn|Barrier|2007|page=230}} and commissioned Dorothy Ann Blank to develop the story.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Crafton|first=Donald|date=1989|title=The Last Night in the Nursery: Walt Disney's ''Peter Pan''|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BT1AAQAAIAAJ&q=dorothy+ann+blank+peter+pan+snow+white|journal=[[The Velvet Light Trap]]|volume=24|page=35|access-date=November 4, 2023|via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> In January 1939, Disney signed a £5,000 contract with the hospital,{{sfn|Williams|Denney|2004|page=164}} and by May of that year, as the story work was in the preliminary stages, he had several animators in mind for some of the characters{{snd}}[[Bill Tytla]] was considered for the pirates, [[Norm Ferguson (animator)|Norman Ferguson]] for Nana, and [[Fred Moore (animator)|Fred Moore]] for Tinker Bell.{{sfn|Barrier|2007|page=230}}

During this time, many possible interpretations of the story were explored. In the earliest treatment, written by Blank on April 14, 1939, the film would start by telling Peter Pan's [[backstory]], which was based on Barrie's 1906 book ''[[Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens]]''. However, during a story meeting the following month, Disney decided that they "ought to get right into the story itself, where Peter Pan comes to the house to get his shadow. That's where the story picks up. How Peter came to be is really another story."<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas" /> Disney also explored the idea of opening the film in Never Land with Peter coming to Wendy's house to kidnap her as a mother for the Lost Boys. Eventually, it was decided that the kidnapping plot was too dark, and Disney went back to Barrie's original play, in which Peter comes to get his shadow back and Wendy herself is eager to see Never Land.<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas" />

By early 1940,<ref name="YouCanFly" /> [[David S. Hall (art director)|David Hall]], who had also worked on ''[[Alice in Wonderland (1951 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'', created first exploratory storyboards and concept art for ''Peter Pan''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.waltdisney.org/blog/revisiting-never-land-celebrating-65-years-peter-pan|last=Benton|first=Jenna|title=Revisiting Never Land: Celebrating 65 Years of ''Peter Pan''|publisher=[[Walt Disney Family Museum]]|date=February 2, 2017|access-date=November 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124152325/https://www.waltdisney.org/blog/revisiting-never-land-celebrating-65-years-peter-pan|archive-date=November 24, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Later that year, Disney personally attempted to contact Maude Adams, who by then had retired from acting and was teaching drama at [[Stephens College]].{{sfn|Burnes|Viets|Butler|2002|page=31}} Disney notified her of his plans for an animated feature, and requested for her to view an early reel of the film that the studio had produced for her approval. He further affirmed that his studio would send the necessary screening equipment to [[Columbia College (Missouri)|Columbia College]] for the presentation and that it could be open to any Stephens College student or faculty member interested in attending.<ref name="Korkis">{{cite web|last=Korkis|first=Jim|url=https://www.mouseplanet.com/13177/How_Maude_Adams_Influenced_Disneys_Peter_Pan|title=How Maude Adams Influenced Disney's Peter Pan|website=MousePlanet|date=June 1, 2022|access-date=January 20, 2023}}</ref> Adams, however, rejected Disney's proposal. In a 1941 studio memo to [[Kay Kamen]], he wrote: "She wouldn't even give me the courtesy of looking at our reel. Her reasons were to the effect that 'Peter whom she created was to her real life and blood, while another's creation of this character would only be a ghost to her'. It seems pretty silly and from my point of view, I would say that Miss Adams is simply living in the past."{{sfn|Burnes|Viets|Butler|2002|page=31}}

===Production delays===
By 1941, the basic story structure of ''Peter Pan'' was completed,<ref name="YouCanFly" /> but later that year, following the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|bombing of Pearl Harbor]], the United States military took control of [[Walt Disney Animation Studios|Walt Disney Productions]]. It commissioned the studio to produce [[Walt Disney's World War II propaganda production|training and war propaganda films]],<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://archive.org/details/variety146-1942-04/page/n61/mode/1up|title=Disney Cartoons Remaining at RKO; Reissues Plans|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|page=6|date=April 8, 1942|access-date=January 19, 2023|via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> thus pre-production work on ''Peter Pan'', as well as on ''[[Alice in Wonderland (1951 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'' (1951), was suspended.{{sfn|Thomas|1994|pp=175–177}} However, the [[Bank of America]] allowed for production on ''Peter Pan'', along with ''[[The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad#The Wind in the Willows|The Wind in the Willows]]'' (1949), to continue during [[World War II]].{{sfn|Gabler|2006|p=490}} After the war had ended, pre-production of the film resumed with [[Jack Kinney]] as director. At the time, Kinney had considered leaving Walt Disney Productions for the [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer cartoon studio]], but wartime restrictions prevented it. Since he did not want Kinney to get out of his contract, Disney appointed Kinney to direct ''Peter Pan''.<ref>{{cite interview|last1=Barrier|first1=Michael|last2=Gray|first2=Milton|url=http://www.michaelbarrier.com/Interviews/Kinney1976/Kinney1976.html|title=Jack Kinney and Jane Kinney (1976)|website=MichaelBarrier.com|date=February 11, 2016|access-date=August 25, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230411222333/http://www.michaelbarrier.com/Interviews/Kinney1976/Kinney1976.html|archive-date=April 11, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>

Impatient with the delays, Disney asked Kinney to work on sequences consecutively rather than finishing the entire script before it was storyboarded, so that a scene would be approved at a morning story meeting and then immediately put into development. Six months later, during a storyboard meeting, Kinney presented a two-and-a-half-hour presentation, during which Disney sat silently and then stated, "You know, I've been thinking about ''[[Cinderella (1950 film)|Cinderella]]''."{{sfn|Gabler|2006|p=460}}

===Return to actual production===
By 1947, Walt Disney Productions' financial health started to improve again.{{sfn|Barrier|2007|p=[https://archive.org/details/animatedmanlifeo00barr/page/204/mode/2up 205]}} Around this time, Disney acknowledged the need for sound economic policies, but emphasized to his financial backers that slashing production would be suicidal to the studio. In order to restore the studio to profitability, Disney expressed his desire to return to producing full-length animated films. By then, three animated projects—''Cinderella'', ''Alice in Wonderland'', and ''Peter Pan''—were in development. Disney had felt the characters in ''Alice in Wonderland'' and ''Peter Pan'' were too cold, but because ''Cinderella'' (1950) contained similar elements when compared to ''Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs'' (1937), he decided to [[greenlight]] ''Cinderella''.{{sfn|Thomas|1994|p=209}} In May 1949, ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' reported that ''Peter Pan'' had been placed back into production.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://archive.org/details/variety174-1949-05/page/n59/mode/2up|title='Pan' Start Gives Disney Record 6 Features Lensing|magazine=Variety|page=5|date=May 11, 1949|access-date=November 12, 2020|via=Internet Archive}}</ref>

The scene in the nursery went through many alterations. In one version, it is Mrs. Darling who finds Peter Pan's shadow and shows it to Mr. Darling, as in the original play. In another version of the film, Nana goes to Never Land with Pan and the Darling children, the story being told through her eyes. In another interpretation of the story, John Darling is left behind for being too serious, practical and boring, but story artist [[Ralph Wright]] convinced Disney to have John go with the others to Never Land. This adaptation also included Wendy bringing her Peter Pan picture book and Peter and the children eating an "imaginary dinner".<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas" /> At one point, a party in Peter's hideout was conceived at which Tinker Bell becomes humiliated and, in her rage, tells Captain Hook the location of Peter Pan's hideout of her own free will. However, Disney felt that this story was contrary to Tinker Bell's character; instead, he had Captain Hook kidnapping Tinker Bell and persuading her to tell him. In Barrie's play, Captain Hook puts poison in Peter's dose of medicine and Tinker Bell saves Peter by drinking the poison herself, only to be revived by the applause of the theater audience. After much debate, Disney discarded this story development, fearing it would be difficult to achieve in a film.<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas" />

In earlier scripts, there were more scenes involving the pirates and mermaids that were similar to those with the dwarfs in ''Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs''. Ultimately, these scenes were cut for pacing reasons.<ref name="AudioCommentary">{{cite AV media notes|author=[[Roy E. Disney]]|title=Audio commentary|location=''Peter Pan'' Platinum Edition DVD|publisher=[[Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment]]|year=2007|type=Bonus feature}}</ref> The film concept was also a bit darker at one point than that of the finished product; for example, there were scenes involving Captain Hook being eaten by the crocodile like in the original play, the Darling family mourning over their lost children and Pan and the children discovering the pirates' treasure loaded with [[booby trap]]s.<ref name="PeterPanThatAlmostWas"/>

===Casting===
[[File:The Walt Disney Christmas Show Bobby Driscoll 1951.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Bobby Driscoll]] portraying Peter Pan in ''The Walt Disney Christmas Show'' (1951).]]
Walt Disney originally wanted to cast [[Mary Martin]] as Peter Pan, but Roy Disney disagreed, finding Martin's voice "too heavy, matured and sophisticated".{{efn|Martin would later portray Peter Pan in the 1954 [[Peter Pan (1954 musical)|Broadway production]] of the original play.}} [[Jean Arthur]] also approached Walt Disney to consider her for the role.{{sfn|Gabler|2006|page=490}} [[Bobby Driscoll]], who was Disney's first contract [[child actor]] and had previously starred in such films as ''[[Song of the South]]'' (1946), ''[[So Dear to My Heart]]'' (1948), and ''[[Treasure Island (1950 film)|Treasure Island]]'' (1950), was ultimately cast.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.waltdisney.org/blog/once-youve-grown-you-can-never-come-back|last=Pepper|first=Jeffrey|title=Once You've Grown Up You Can Never Come Back|publisher=[[Walt Disney Family Museum]]|date=November 14, 2011|access-date=February 2, 2023}}</ref> This was the first time that a male actor was cast as Peter Pan, breaking a tradition of women portraying him in both films and stage productions.<ref name="YouCanFly" /> Driscoll also provided some of the live-action reference for the character.<ref name="PeterPanCharacterHistory" /> ''Peter Pan'' was Driscoll's last Disney film, as his contract with the studio was abruptly terminated shortly after its release.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Korkis|first=Jim|url=https://www.mouseplanet.com/13178/Bobby_Driscoll_at_Disney|title=Bobby Driscoll at Disney|website=MousePlanet|date=June 8, 2022|access-date=February 2, 2023}}</ref>

For the role of Wendy, Disney wanted a "gentle and gracefully feminine" voice, which he found in [[Kathryn Beaumont]],<ref name="YouCanFly" /> who had previously voiced the [[Portrayals of Alice in Wonderland#Disney|title character]] in ''[[Alice in Wonderland (1951 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'' (1951) and had just finished working on the film.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dvdizzy.com/kathrynbeaumont-interview.html|title=Kathryn Beaumont Interview: UltimateDisney.com Talks with the Voice and Model for Alice and Wendy|last=Joy|first=Renata|date=February 23, 2007|website=DVDizzy.com|access-date=February 3, 2023}}</ref> Disney initially offered the role of Captain Hook to [[Cary Grant]], which the latter was "intrigued with",{{sfn|Gabler|2006|page=490}} but eventually [[Hans Conried]] was cast as both Hook<ref name="CaptainHookVillainsHistory" /> and, in keeping the tradition of the stage play, George Darling.{{sfn|Bohn|2017|p=154}}

===Animation===
====Live-action reference====
As with previous Disney animated features since ''Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs'' (1937), a live-action version with the actors performing to a prerecorded dialogue track was filmed to serve as an aid to animators.<ref name="AudioCommentary" /> [[Margaret Kerry]] received a call to audition to serve as the live-action reference for Tinker Bell.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Fine|first=Audrey|url=http://www.seventeen.com/celebrity/a11636/margaret-kerry/|title=Teen Talks To: Margaret Kerry, a.k.a. Tinker Bell|magazine=[[Seventeen (American magazine)|Seventeen]]|date=March 14, 2007|access-date=August 25, 2017}}</ref> For the live-action reference, Kerry said she had to hold out her arms and pretend to fly for all the scenes requiring it.<ref name="YouCanFly" /> Additionally, Kerry served as reference for one of the mermaids, along with Connie Hilton and [[June Foray]].<ref>{{cite interview|subject=Margaret Kerry|title=Margaret Kerry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zOzpwaDTR2wC&pg=PA182|interviewer=Jim Korkis|work=Walt's People—Volume 9|date=October 2003|publisher=[[Xlibris]]|pages=177–182|isbn=978-1-450-08746-9|via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref>{{Self-published inline|certain=yes|date=December 2017}}

At the same time, the studio was looking for an actor to portray Peter Pan, to which Kerry suggested her dancing teacher [[Roland Dupree]]. He was interviewed and eventually won the role,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://accessreel.com/article/roland-dupree-peter-pan/|title=Roland Dupree – Peter Pan|website=AccessReel.com|access-date=August 25, 2017}}</ref> providing visual reference for the flying and action sequences. [[Bobby Driscoll]] also served as the live-action reference model for Peter Pan, although he was mainly used for the close-up scenes. [[Kathryn Beaumont]], who was the voice of Wendy, performed the live-action reference footage for the character.<ref name="YouCanFly" />

[[Hans Conried]] completed the voice work over the course of a few days, but served as the live-action reference for two and a half years.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gargiulo|first=Suzanne|title=Hans Conried: A Biography; With a Filmography and a Listing of Radio, Television, Stage and Voice Work|chapter=Peter Pan, The Twonky, and Dr. T.|page=78|publisher=[[McFarland & Company]]|year=2002|isbn=978-0-786-41338-6|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PNkE0c78qYQC&q=hans+conried+captain+hook&pg=PA79|via=Google Books}}</ref>

====Character animation====
In a 1978 TV special ''From Fantasia to Fantasyland'', [[Milt Kahl]] stated he had wanted to animate Captain Hook but was instead assigned to animate Peter Pan and the Darling children; he claimed he was "outmaneuvered".<ref>{{cite AV media |people=Dixon, Terence |title=From Fantasia to Fantasyland |year=1978 |location=London |publisher=[[Thames Television]] |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qG4CQT9v4c |time=21:30 |access-date=August 25, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260424181109/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qG4CQT9v4c |archive-date=April 24, 2026 |url-status=live |via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref> During production, while animating Peter Pan, Kahl claimed that the hardest thing to animate was a character floating in mid-air.<ref name="YouCanFly" /> While observing the animation of Peter Pan, Disney complained that the animators had let too many of Bobby Driscoll's facial features find their way into the character design, telling Kahl that "[t]hey are too masculine, too old. There is something wrong there." Kahl replied, "You want to know what's wrong!?... What's wrong is that they don't have any talent in the place."{{sfn|Gabler|2006|p=460}}

[[Frank Thomas (animator)|Frank Thomas]] was assigned to animate Captain Hook, though he faced conflicting creative visions of the character. Story artist Ed Penner viewed Hook as "a very foppish, not strong, dandy-type, who loved all the finery. Kind of a con man. [Co-director Gerry] Geronimi saw him as an [[Ernest Torrence]]: a mean, heavy sort of character who used his hook menacingly." When Disney saw Thomas' first test scenes, he said, "Well, that last scene has something I like I think you're beginning to get him. I think we better wait and let Frank go on a little further."{{sfn|Barrier|1999|p=551}}{{sfn|Canemaker|2001|p=190}} Because Thomas could not animate every scene of Hook, certain sequences were given to [[Wolfgang Reitherman]], such as Hook trying to escape the crocodile at Skull Rock.{{sfn|Canemaker|2001|pp=45–46}}

[[Ollie Johnston]] animated Mr. Smee. To best capture his comedic yet fear-ridden, sycophantic personality, Johnston used a variation of the Dwarf design from ''Snow White'', and had Mr. Smee blink repeatedly. Johnston's former mentor, Fred Moore, worked in his unit as a character animator for Smee's minor scenes. Moore also animated the mermaids and the Lost Boys. The film would be Moore's final work as he died in a traffic accident on November 22, 1952.{{sfn|Canemaker|2001|pp=225–226}}

==Reception==
===Critical reaction===
''Peter Pan'' received generally positive reviews from critics upon release, some of whom praised the animation but felt it veered too far from the play.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Liu |first=Narayan |date=October 16, 2020 |title=Report: Disney's Peter Pan and Wendy Eyes Newcomer as Tiger Lily |url=https://www.cbr.com/report-disneys-peter-pan-and-wendy-eyes-newcomer-as-tiger-lily/ |access-date=June 26, 2024 |work=[[Comic Book Resources]] |quote=Disney's original adaptation of J. M. Barrie's 1904 play ... premiered in 1953 to a generally positive reception.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Knight |first=Kristina |date=November 20, 2019 |title=How to Stream Peter Pan: Your Family Viewing Guide |url=https://heavy.com/streaming/2019/11/stream-peter-pan/ |access-date=June 26, 2024 |work=[[Heavy (website)|Heavy]] |quote=Peter Pan received mostly positive reviews upon its release}}</ref> [[Bosley Crowther]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' criticized the film's lack of faithfulness to the original play, claiming it "has the story but not the spirit of ''Peter Pan'' as it was plainly conceived by its author and is usually played on the stage". Nevertheless, he praised the colors are "more exciting and the technical features of the job, such as the synchronization of voices with the animation of lips, are very good".<ref>{{cite news |last=Crowther |first=Bosley|author-link=Bosley Crowther|title=The Screen in Review: Disney's 'Peter Pan' Bows |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1953/02/12/archives/the-screen-disneys-peter-pan-bows-fulllength-color-cartoon-an.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=23 |date=February 12, 1953 |access-date=August 25, 2017}}</ref> However, ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine gave the film a highly favorable review, writing "it is a lively feature-length Technicolor excursion into a world that glows with an exhilarating charm and a gentle joyousness."<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,817903,00.html |title=Cinema: The New Pictures |magazine=Time |page=78 |date=February 2, 1953 |access-date=May 22, 2010}}</ref> ''[[The Chicago Tribune]]'' wrote: "The backgrounds are delightfully picturesque, the music only so-so. The film is designed for broad effect, with the accent of comedy. I'm sure the youngsters who grow up with cartoons will be right at home with all the characters."<ref>{{cite news |last=Tinee |first=Mae |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/63170522/clipped-from-the-chicago-tribune/ |title=4 Top Grade Movies Open in February |work=[[Chicago Tribune]]|at=Section 2, p. 3 |date=March 1, 1953 |access-date=November 13, 2020 |via=Newspapers.com}} {{Open access}}</ref> ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' described the film as a "feature cartoon of enchanting quality. The music score is fine, highlighting the constant buzz of action and comedy, but the songs are less impressive than usually encountered in such a Disney presentation."<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Film Reviews: Peter Pan |url=https://archive.org/details/variety189-1953-01 |magazine=Variety |page=[https://archive.org/details/variety189-1953-01/page/n299/mode/2up 6] |date=January 14, 1953 |access-date=August 25, 2017 |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> ''[[Harrison's Reports]]'' felt the film was "another Walt Disney masterpiece. Giving the film {{frac|3|1|2}} stars out of 4, [[Gene Siskel]] of the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' noted the "drawing of Tinkerbelle [''sic''] and the flamboyance of Captain Hook" as well as the "quality music mixed with appropriate animation" were the film's major highlights.<ref>{{cite news |last=Siskel |first=Gene|author-link=Gene Siskel|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1989-07-14-8902190392-story.html|title=Bright Dialogue Sparks ''When Harry Met Sally''|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|date=July 14, 1989|access-date=September 22, 2023}}</ref> [[Michael Jackson]] cited ''Peter Pan'' as his favorite film, and from it he derived the name of his estate, [[Neverland Ranch]], in [[Santa Barbara, California]], where he had a private [[amusement park]]. ===Controversy===
''Peter Pan'' has been criticized since at least the 1990s for its broadly stereotypical treatment of Native Americans. 

In 1995, [[Eric Goldberg (animator)|Eric Goldberg]], director of that year's Disney animated romance [[Pocahontas (1995 film)|''Pocahontas'']], expressed his belief that "all the Indians [in the 1953 film] were caricatures".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sharkey |first=Betsy |date=1995-06-11 |title=Moving Beyond Teepees and Totem Poles|newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/06/11/arts/beyong-teepees-and-totem-poles.html |access-date=2023-08-26}}</ref>

In particular, the song "[[What Made the Red Man Red?]]" has been removed from television airings of the film<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2018-06-24 |title=Digital Spy |url=http://www.digitalspy.com/movies/feature/a838617/disney-movie-racist-moments/ |url-status=live Animator [[Marc Davis (animator)|Marc Davis]] was quoted in the 2007 audio commentary: "I'm not sure we would have done the Indians if we were making this movie now. And if we had, we wouldn't do them the way we did back then."<ref name="AudioCommentary" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Korkis|first=Jim|url=https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/neverland-tribe/|title=Neverland Tribe|date=May 15, 2020|access-date=December 4, 2020|website=[[Cartoon Research]]}}</ref>

===Board game===
''Walt Disney's Peter Pan: A Game of Adventure'' (1953) is a Transogram Company Inc. track [[board game]] based upon the film. The game was one of many toys that exploited the popularity of Walt Disney's post–[[World War II]] movies.<ref>Rich, Mark. ''Warman's 101 Greatest Baby Boomer Toys''. kp books, 2005. p. 72.</ref> The object of the game is to be the first player to travel from the Darlings' house to [[Neverland]] and back to the Darlings' house.

Play begins at the Darlings' house in the upper left hand corner of the game board. Each player moves, in turn, the number of spaces along the track indicated by his spin of the dial. When a player reaches the Never Isle, he selects a character from the film (Peter, Wendy, Michael, or John) and receives the instruction card for that character. The player follows his chosen character's track on the board, obeying instructions upon the character's card. The player is also obligated to follow any instructions on those spaces he lands upon after spinning the dial during the course of his turn at play. The first player who travels from Never Land to Skull Rock and along the Stardust Trail to Captain Hook's ship, and returns to the Darlings' house is declared the winner.

The board game makes an appearance in the 1968 version of ''[[Yours, Mine and Ours (1968 film)|Yours, Mine and Ours]]'' as a Christmas present.

===Sequels===
This was Disney's first ''Peter Pan'' film. In the early 2000s, a ''Peter Pan'' franchise was spawned, involving a number of other animated releases. The franchise also included:
* ''[[Return to Never Land]]'': Released theatrically in 2002, and a direct-sequel to ''Peter Pan''.
* The ''[[Tinker Bell (film series)|Tinker Bell]]'' film series: A spin-off and prequel to the ''Peter Pan'' films. [[Disneytoon Studios]] produced a number of ''Tinker Bell'' films, including six feature-length straight-to-home video films, and two shorts.
* The television series ''[[Jake and the Never Land Pirates]]'' includes Hook and Smee as main characters, and is set in Never Land, some time after the events of ''Peter Pan''. Tick-Tock the Crocodile appears as a recurring character in the series. Peter, Tinker Bell, Wendy, Michael and John also appear as guest characters.
